newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Call-back seen slashing HK Telecom's market share.
newsitem.headline: Call-back seen slashing HK Telecom's market share.

text.p: Call-back services may slash Hongkong Telecommunications Ltd share of the international market to 65 percent by the end of its fiscal year on March 31, Lloyd Fischer, BZW Asia's head of regional telecommunications research said on Thursday.
In a briefing on Asian regional telecoms, Fischer said Hongkong Telecom's interim results last year had unveiled a market share of 85 percent in call origination from Hong Kong.
He said this could fall to 65 percent when it reported its full-year results, and said it might fall to 50 percent in calendar 1997.
Fischer said the decline was part of an international trend towards a shake-up that may see the international traffic settlement system collapse in as little as 18 months.
In a report on Asian Regional Telecommunications, he forecast the breakdown of the "international cartel" of telecoms monopolies and duopolies.
"The only real issue is timing," Fischer told reporters.
"We anticipate the system will eventually collapse within an 18-month to three-year time frame."
Hongkong Telecom has lost its monopoly on domestic Hong Kong calls but its monopoly on international calls is not due to expire until 2006, although competitors are nibbling at the edges.
Fischer said Hongkong Telecom was "moderately" vulnerable" to the impending shake-up. Most vulnerable were PT Indonesian Satellite Corp and Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co.
Least Vulnerable were Thai-listed TelecomAsia Corp and Thai Telephone & Telecommunication Plc, Fischer said.
He forecast the carriage of international traffic would turn into a commodity-type business.

"Although there will be tremendous growth in the industry, it may start to look more like the airline industry, where only a few efficient service-orientated companies -- and equipment companies -- are able to make profits," Fischer said.
He said the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) wanted to cut an estimated US$5.5 billion deficit incurred by U.S. carriers in settling international calls.
"This sum represents the payment by U.S. carriers for the excess minutes of traffic that the U.S sent to other countries over and above what it received," Fischer said.
World Trade Organisation (WTO) talks were increasing pressure on Asia to open its markets up, he said.
Other factors contributing to the collapse included more use of alternative systems such as call-back which "will turn the market into a highly competitive commodity business", he said.
Call-back systems involve bypassing high tariff rates by allowing a call from a high-tariff country to be made to a "call-back switch" in another lower-tariff country.
The call-back switch initiates the call, and the customer pays a lower fee to the call-back carrier.
Call-back was illegal in some countries, but it was difficult to stop customers from using the service, he said.
Asian telecoms with high accounting and tariff rates, a high percentage of revenue derived from international traffic and a growing traffic imbalance would be the most vulnerable, he said.
Fischer said some carriers' share of international traffic was falling at an unprecedented level.
His comments coincided with news of two Hong Kong-based competitors announcing international direct dialling (IDD) charges to undercut Hongkong Telecom's charges.
A Hongkong Telecom spokesman said some customers were opting for callback, but said Hongkong Telecom offered "the best quality service and the clearest line".
The spokesman declined to comment on its market share.
